body.text: Tax payable, in the context of Canada's SR&ED program, is the federal Part I income tax a claimant owes under the Income Tax Act. Non-refundable SR&ED investment tax credits first reduce Part I tax otherwise payable, unused credits carry back 3 years or forward 20 years, and recaptured ITCs are added to tax payable.

This report provides a comprehensive legal, technical, and financial audit of the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive regime and complementary innovation funding programs in Canada as of November 2026.

Canada's R&D tax landscape underwent its most significant structural expansion in over three decades with the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Incorporating measures first announced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024), refined in the Department of Finance's August 15, 2025 legislative proposals, and expanded in Budget 2025 (which projected a net federal fiscal cost of $293 million over five years from 2025–2026 through 2029–2030 for the further limit expansion), Bill C-15 doubled the federal enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (superseding the interim $4,500,000 proposal), broadened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out band from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the enhanced 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average annual revenue phase-out ($15 million to $75 million), permitted Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) to elect into the revenue-based phase-out, and restored capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs for property acquired or leased after December 15, 2024. Concurrently, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026 (using Form T1322), while at the provincial level, Québec replaced its legacy R&D tax measures with the consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, and British Columbia enacted Bill 2 on April 16, 2026, making its 10% SR&ED tax credit permanent and doubling its refundable expenditure limit to $6,000,000.

For corporate tax directors, R&D auditors, and legal counsel, the critical operational takeaway is that vintage cutoff dates govern every calculation straddling the 2024–2026 transition. The enhanced $6,000,000 expenditure limit, expanded $15 million–$75 million phase-out range, and ECPC eligibility apply to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (meaning calendar-year 2025 and 2026 corporate returns qualify in full), whereas the restoration of capital expenditures, SUE, and equipment lease costs applies on a transaction-date basis to depreciable property acquired (and available for use) or lease amounts first becoming payable after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024). Furthermore, despite the CRA's August 2021 administrative shift toward a streamlined "Why" and "How" eligibility framework, the Federal Court of Appeal has repeatedly confirmed in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D Inc. v. The Queen (2022 FCA 72) that the five-question common-law test established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (1998) remains the binding legal standard in Canadian courts.

body.text: Section 1: Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 The Dual-Mechanism Framework: Section 37 vs. Section 127

Canada's federal SR&ED Tax Incentive Program is the largest single source of federal support for industrial research and development, distributing over $3 billion annually according to industry estimates. Unlike direct discretionary grants, the SR&ED program is an entitlement codified in the federal Income Tax Act (the Act) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (the Regulations), jointly administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) (which conducts technical and financial reviews and processes claims) and the Department of Finance Canada (which formulates legislative tax policy).
Calculating a federal SR&ED claim requires executing two legally distinct but interconnected statutory computations:

items: The Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures: Governed by subsection 37(1) of the Act, this mechanism allows a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada to pool current and (for property acquired after December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada that are related to a business of the taxpayer. The taxpayer may deduct all or any portion of the available pool balance in computing net business income for the current taxation year, or carry forward any undeducted positive pool balance indefinitely to reduce business income in future taxation years.

The Section 127 and Section 127.1 Investment Tax Credit (ITC): Governed by subsections 127(5) to 127(36) and section 127.1 of the Act, this mechanism generates a percentage tax credit (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) calculated on the taxpayer's qualified SR&ED expenditures for the year. Depending on the taxpayer's legal status and expenditure type, the ITC may be applied to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable, refunded in cash (up to 100% or 40%), carried back 3 taxation years, or carried forward 20 taxation years.

body.text: A foundational principle of Canadian R&D tax auditing is that "allowable SR&ED expenditure" (for Section 37 deduction purposes) and "qualified expenditure" (for Section 127 ITC purposes) are distinct statutory concepts. Certain outlays—such as payments under non-arm's length SR&ED contracts where no Form T1146 transfer is executed, the 20% excluded portion of arm's-length contractor and third-party payments, or acquisitions of used depreciable capital property after December 15, 2024—are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool but do not qualify for Section 127 ITCs. Conversely, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) (55% of the eligible salary base under the Proxy Method) and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) additions (25% of capital cost per term) are included in Section 127 qualified expenditures to earn ITCs, but are strictly barred from entering the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool.
1.2 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED: Subsection 248(1)

Every federal and provincial R&D tax claim in Canada stands or falls on the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (added to subsection 248(1) in 1996, having previously resided in Regulation 2900). Under subsection 248(1), "scientific research and experimental development" means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statutory architecture divides work into four eligible categories (paragraphs (a) through (d)) and seven explicitly excluded categories (paragraphs (e) through (k)), as detailed in the table below.

body.text: Technical Nuances of Paragraphs (a)–(d) vs. Paragraphs (e)–(k)

In Canadian SR&ED audits, the overwhelming majority of industrial claims fall under paragraph (c) (Experimental Development) coupled with paragraph (d) (Support Work). The statutory text and the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentives (dated August 13, 2021) establish three critical legal boundaries.

First, claimants must distinguish between an advancement of underlying technology and mere product novelty. Achieving commercial novelty, innovation, uniqueness, feature enhancement, or increased functionality of a product or process does not in itself demonstrate scientific or technological advancement. Similarly, acquiring publicly available knowledge or existing industry know-how—whether through employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring external experts or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge—does not meet the requirement of attempting to achieve a technological advancement. Technological advancement exists where existing design methods are inapplicable, specifications conflict with established standards, parameters lie outside normal operating ranges, or system-level variables create technological uncertainty that a competent professional in the field cannot resolve through standard practice or routine engineering.

Second, incremental improvements and unsuccessful projects qualify. Paragraph (c) explicitly encompasses "incremental improvements" to existing materials, devices, products, or processes, provided those incremental improvements require resolving genuine technological uncertainty through systematic experiment or analysis. Moreover, a project does not need to succeed commercially or technically to qualify; a failed experimental attempt that refutes a hypothesis and generates new scientific or technological knowledge regarding why an approach fails is fully eligible.

Third, the CRA applies a purpose and proportionality test to demarcate paragraph (d) support work from paragraphs (e)–(k) excluded work. Because activities like "testing" and "data collection" appear in both paragraph (d) (eligible support work) and paragraphs (f) and (k) (excluded routine testing and routine data collection), the determinative factor is purpose: why was the work performed20? Support work under paragraph (d) is eligible only after core SR&ED work under paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) has been identified, and only to the extent that the engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research is commensurate with the needs and carried out specifically and directly in support of resolving the scientific or technological uncertainty. Once the scientific or technological advancement is achieved by resolving the associated uncertainties, or the uncertainties are determined to be unresolvable, or the project is terminated for any reason, project completion is reached and the eligibility of all work ceases immediately at that point.

body.text: Section 2: Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures & Section 127 Qualified Expenditures
2.1 Mechanics of the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

The Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures is calculated in Part 3, Section C of Form T661 (lines 400 to 470). Unlike regular business deductions under section 9(1) or Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) under paragraph 20(1)(a), the Section 37 pool operates as a cumulative, running tax account. Individual expenditures lose their year-of-origin identity once admitted to the pool and can be deducted in full, deducted in part, or carried forward indefinitely.
Step-by-Step Computation of the Section 37 Pool (Form T661, Part 3, Section C)

items: Current-Year Allowable SR&ED Expenditures (Line 400): The calculation begins with the sum of allowable current SR&ED expenditures (line 380) and allowable SR&ED capital expenditures on depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (line 390). Current expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(a) encompass salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED (plus directly attributable supervisory, support, and clerical staff under the Traditional Method), materials consumed or transformed in SR&ED, equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, SR&ED contracts performed on the claimant's behalf in Canada, third-party payments to approved entities, and directly related and incremental overhead expenditures when the Traditional Method is elected. Capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) (restored by Bill C-15) encompass the capital cost of new or used depreciable property (other than buildings, leasehold interests in buildings, or land) acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 that is intended to have all or substantially all (ASA, defined as 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life, or 90% or more of its value, used or consumed in performing SR&ED in Canada.

Subtractions for Assistance (Lines 429, 431, 432 — Paragraph 37(1)(d) & (d.1)): The pool is reduced by provincial government assistance (such as provincial R&D tax credits on line 429), other government assistance (such as NRC IRAP or Strategic Innovation Fund / Strategic Response Fund contributions on line 431), non-government assistance (line 432), and any provincial super-allowance benefits (paragraph 37(1)(d.1)) that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at the filing-due date in respect of allowable SR&ED expenditures. Under the Proxy Method, government assistance specifically attributable to overhead expenses is not deducted from the Section 37 pool because overhead expenses themselves are excluded from the pool.

Subtraction for Prior-Year Federal SR&ED ITCs (Line 435 — Paragraph 37(1)(e)): Any federal SR&ED ITC claimed (applied against Part I tax, carried back, or refunded in cash) in the preceding taxation year reduces the current year's Section 37 pool. This creates a one-year deferral mechanism: a federal ITC earned in Year 1 does not reduce the Year 1 Section 37 deduction, but reduces the Section 37 pool in Year 2.
Subtraction for Sale of SR&ED Capital Assets and Other Deductions (Line 440): Proceeds from the disposition of SR&ED capital property and other statutory reductions decrease the pool.

Additions for Repayments of Assistance, Prior-Year Pool Balance, Amalgamations, and ITC Recapture (Lines 445, 450, 452, 453): Line 445 (paragraph 37(1)(c)) adds repayments of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the Section 37 pool. Line 450 adds the ending Section 37 pool balance carried forward from the prior taxation year. Line 452 adds pool balances transferred upon a qualifying amalgamation or winding-up. Line 453 (paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and (c.3)) adds the amount of any federal SR&ED ITC recapture (or partnership ITC recapture excess) included in the taxpayer's Part I tax in the prior taxation year.

Negative Pool Balance Rule (Paragraph 12(1)(v) and Paragraph 37(1)(c.1)): If the net balance of the Section 37 pool at the end of the taxation year is negative—which commonly occurs when a claimant deducts its entire Section 37 pool in Year 1 and then must subtract the Year 1 federal ITC on Line 435 in Year 2 while having minimal Year 2 SR&ED spending—the negative balance must be brought into net business income under paragraph 12(1)(v) on Schedule 18. That exact income inclusion is then added back to the pool under paragraph 37(1)(c.1) so that the opening pool balance for the subsequent taxation year is reset to nil ($0).

Current-Year Deduction and Indefinite Carryforward (Lines 455, 460, 470): If the net available pool on Line 455 is positive, the claimant elects how much to deduct on Line 460 (which flows to Line 411 of T2 Schedule 1). For any deduction attributable to restored capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b), subsection 37(6) deems the amount claimed to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed in respect of the property. The remaining balance on Line 470 carries forward indefinitely.

body.text: Impact of Loss Restriction Events (Acquisition of Control)

Under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1) (as amended by Bill C-15 to cover paragraph 37(1)(b) capital property acquired after December 15, 2024), when a corporation undergoes a loss restriction event (such as an acquisition of control of a corporation or a change in the majority-interest beneficiary of a trust), a deemed taxation year-end is triggered immediately prior to the acquisition, and the corporation's undeducted Section 37 pool balance is reduced to nil. The pre-acquisition Section 37 pool balance can only be reinstated and deducted in post-acquisition taxation years if two statutory conditions are met:

items: The specific business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on by the corporation for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit throughout the post-acquisition taxation year; and
The deduction is limited to the corporation's income for the post-acquisition taxation year (before making any Section 37 pool deduction) derived from that same business or a similar business.

body.text: 2.2 Mechanics of Section 127 Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures

Whereas Section 37 governs income deductions, Part 4 of Form T661 (lines 500 to 570) computes Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures under subsection 127(9) to determine the base on which federal Investment Tax Credits are earned. Unlike the Section 37 pool, the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool is an annual calculation that does not carry over from one taxation year to the next; instead, it converts into an ITC on T2 Schedule 31 (or Form T2038(IND)).

Starting from Line 400 (Total Allowable SR&ED Expenditures), Part 4 adds the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 502), Shared-Use Equipment claims (Line 504), prior-year unpaid non-wage amounts paid in the year (Line 500), and qualified expenditures transferred from non-arm's length performers via Form T1146 (Line 508). It then subtracts provincial, federal, and non-government assistance and contract payments (Lines 513–518), current non-wage expenditures unpaid 180 days after year-end (Line 520), payments to non-taxable suppliers (Line 528), the 20% disallowed portion of arm's-length contracts and third-party payments (Line 529), prescribed expenditures such as used capital property (Line 530/532), expenditures tied to tax-exempt income (Line 533/535), and non-arm's length adjustments and transfers (Lines 538–544). Finally, repayments of assistance and contract payments made in the year are added on Line 560 to arrive at Line 570. Under the CRA's Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures Policy and Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, while repayments on Line 560 are included in Line 570 and generate an ITC at the rate that applied when the assistance originally reduced the claim, repayments are not "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) and therefore the ITC earned on repayments is non-refundable in the year of repayment.

body.text: Section 3: Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Phase-Outs, Refundability, and Carryovers (Post-Bill C-15)
3.1 The 35% Enhanced ITC vs. 15% Basic ITC Rate Structure

Under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(10.1) of the Income Tax Act, Canada operates a two-tier federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit rate system. The basic ITC rate of 15% (which was reduced from 20% effective January 1, 2014) applies to all eligible claimants—including large corporations, foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries, Canadian public corporations (on expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit or if not qualifying as an ECPC), CCPCs (on expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit), sole proprietors (individuals), partners of partnerships, and beneficiaries of trusts.

The enhanced ITC rate of 35%—which consists of the 15% basic rate plus an additional 20% enhancement under subsection 127(10.1)—is earned on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the claimant's annual Expenditure Limit. Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, eligibility for the 35% enhanced rate applies to both Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs).
3.2 Doubling of the Expenditure Limit to $6,000,000 and Phase-Out Mechanics

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced rate was $3,000,000 (generating a maximum enhanced ITC of $1,050,000), and was restricted exclusively to CCPCs. Although the 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed increasing this limit to $4,500,000, Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 increased the maximum annual expenditure limit to $6,000,000 effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, doubling the maximum annual enhanced federal ITC to $2,100,000. Department of Finance Canada budget estimates project the fiscal impact of expanding the limit from $4.5 million to $6.0 million at $3 million in 2025–2026, $70 million in 2026–2027, $85 million in 2027–2028, $65 million in 2028–2029, and $70 million in 2029–2030, for a total five-year cost of $293 million.

If a corporation's taxation year is shorter than 51 weeks, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is prorated by the ratio of the number of days in the short taxation year to 365 (for example, a 273-day short taxation year yields a prorated maximum expenditure limit of $6,000,000 × 273 ÷ 365 = $4,487,671). Furthermore, associated corporations (under section 256) must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit and allocate it among group members using T2 Schedule 49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). Under subsection 127(10.4), if an associated group fails to file an allocation agreement within 30 days of a written request by the CRA, the Minister allocates the expenditure limit among the corporations.
1. The Standard CCPC Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (Subsection 127(10.2))
For a CCPC that does not make a revenue election under subsection 127(10.31) or (10.32), subsection 127(10.2) calculates the annual expenditure limit using the following statutory formula:

In this formula, variable A is nil ($0) if the corporation's taxable capital employed in Canada (determined under Part I.3, section 181.2 of the Act, aggregated across the CCPC and all associated corporations for their last taxation year ending in the preceding calendar year) is less than or equal to $15,000,000; in any other case, A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000. body.text: 2. Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and the CCPC Revenue Election (Subsections 127(10.6), 127(10.31), and 127(10.32))

To prevent Canadian technology and life sciences companies from losing the 35% refundable SR&ED credit upon listing on a stock exchange or raising large institutional venture capital rounds, Bill C-15 introduced two structural mechanisms effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.

First, under subsection 127(10.6), Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) can access the $6,000,000 expenditure limit and earn the 35% enhanced refundable ITC. Instead of using Part I.3 taxable capital employed in Canada, an ECPC's variable A in the $6,000,000 × [($60M − A) ÷ $60M] formula is calculated using the average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of the corporation (and all members of its consolidated group) over the 3 preceding fiscal years. The ECPC expenditure limit begins to decrease when 3-year average annual revenue exceeds $15,000,000 and reaches nil at $75,000,000.

Second, because taxable capital under section 181.2 includes the full balance-sheet carrying value of share capital (including preferred share rounds), contributed surplus, loans, advances, convertible notes, and debt outstanding for more than 365 days (minus accounting deficits and the investment allowance), capital-intensive pre-revenue startups frequently exceed $15,000,000 (or $75,000,000) in prior-year taxable capital while generating little or no revenue. Under subsection 127(10.31) (for unassociated CCPCs) and subsection 127(10.32) (for associated CCPC groups electing jointly), a CCPC may elect on the prescribed form to determine its expenditure limit under the subsection 127(10.6) 3-year average annual revenue method ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000 revenue taper) instead of the taxable capital method. Under subsection 127(10.64), if a corporation has fewer than three preceding fiscal years, the average is computed across the available preceding fiscal years, with any fiscal year shorter than 51 weeks annualized.

3.4 Carryback, Carryforward, Partnerships, and Loss Restrictions on ITCs

Under subsection 127(5), any non-refundable portion of an SR&ED ITC (or refundable ITC that the taxpayer chooses not to have refunded) is first applied to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable for the current taxation year. Any unused balance may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years. Under subsection 127(5), the amount carried back to a prior taxation year is limited to the lesser of (i) the portion of the current-year ITC that was not deductible or refunded in the current year, and (ii) the amount by which Part I tax otherwise payable in that prior year exceeds the ITC already deducted or refunded in that prior year. Unused ITCs expire if not applied against Part I tax within the 20-year carryforward window. Furthermore, upon an acquisition of control of a corporation, carryforwards of pre-acquisition unused ITCs to post-acquisition taxation years, and carrybacks of post-acquisition unused ITCs to pre-acquisition taxation years, are restricted to offsetting Part I tax reasonably attributable to income from the same or a similar business.
Special Rules for Partnerships (SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy)
Because a partnership is not a separate "taxpayer" under the Income Tax Act, special flow-through rules under subsections 96(1) and 127(8) govern partnership SR&ED claims:

items: Mandatory Current-Year Pool Deduction (Paragraph 96(1)(e.1)): A partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37 pool balance to a future fiscal period. The entire available Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures must be deducted in full in computing the partnership's net business income or loss for the fiscal period in which the expenditures were incurred.

Prohibition on Partner Salaries: A partner cannot be an employee of the partnership for income tax purposes; any "salary" or "wages" paid to a partner is treated by the CRA as a distribution of partnership income and is ineligible as an SR&ED salary expenditure.

Exclusion of Specified Members and Limited Partner Loss Restrictions: Under subsection 127(8) and subsection 248(1), a "specified member" of a partnership—which includes any limited partner as well as any passive general partner who is not regularly, continuously, and substantially actively engaged in the partnership's business activities (other than financing) or carrying on a similar business—is precluded from receiving any allocation of the partnership's SR&ED ITC. Furthermore, any portion of a partnership loss disallowed to a limited partner because it includes a Section 37 SR&ED deduction is not allowed to other partners, does not become a limited partnership loss or non-capital loss, and does not affect the adjusted cost base of the limited partner's partnership interest.

Ineligibility for Form T1146 Transfers: Because a partnership is not a "person" or "taxpayer" for the purposes of subsection 127(13), a partnership cannot transfer or receive qualified SR&ED expenditures to or from a non-arm's length party using Form T1146.

4.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method: Election Mechanics and Break-Even Analysis

Under subsection 37(8) and subsection 37(10) of the Act, every SR&ED claimant must elect on Form T661 (Part 3, Section A, Line 160 for the Proxy Method or Line 162 for the Traditional Method) how to compute its SR&ED expenditures and overhead for the taxation year. The choice between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method is made on a year-by-year basis: a claimant may use the Proxy Method in Year 1 and switch to the Traditional Method in Year 2, but once Form T661 is filed for a given taxation year, the method chosen for that year is irrevocable. If a claimant fails to select a method on Form T661, the CRA automatically processes the claim under the Traditional Method.

Under the Proxy Method (Regulation 2900(4)), rather than identifying, tracking, and proving actual overhead costs, the claimant calculates a notional amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base. (Historically, the PPA rate was 65% prior to 2013 and 60% in 2013, reaching 55% for 2014 and all subsequent years). The PPA is added on Line 502 of Form T661 to earn Section 127 ITCs, while the claimant deducts its actual overhead outlays (utilities, shop supplies, clerical wages, employer CPP/EI/benefits, training, travel) as ordinary business expenses under section 9(1) of the Act.

To prevent single-purpose R&D corporations whose expenses consist almost entirely of SR&ED salaries and building rent from claiming a notional 55% PPA that exceeds their actual total non-SR&ED business expenses, subsection 2900(6) of the Regulations imposes an Overall Cap on the PPA calculated by the formula:
Overall PPA cap = A − B − C

In this formula, A is the total of all amounts deducted in computing net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold); B is the sum of all deductions claimed in the year under section 20 (e.g., CCA, interest, bad debts), section 24 (ceasing to carry on business), section 26 (banks), section 30 (improving land for farming), section 32 (insurance agents/brokers), section 37 (the SR&ED expenditure pool deduction itself, Line 411 of Schedule 1), sections 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and section 104 (trusts); and C is the total amount of outlays and expenses incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (building rent/lease costs). In practice, the Regulation 2900(6) overall cap will not restrict the PPA provided the claimant has deducted at least $55 of ordinary non-SR&ED, non-building-rent, non-section-20 business expenses for every $100 of eligible salary in the salary base.

body.text: 4.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employee Caps, and 2026 YMPE Limits

Salaries and wages represent the single largest expenditure category in Canadian SR&ED claims. Under subsection 248(1) and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" means income from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act.
1. Directly Engaged Tasks and Inclusions vs. Exclusions

Whether an employee is "directly engaged in SR&ED" is a question of fact determined by the actual hands-on tasks performed, not by the employee's job title. Directly engaged tasks encompass hands-on experimental work (formulating hypotheses, designing experiments, writing experimental code, building trial prototypes, running tests, and analyzing results); direct, first-line technical supervision of hands-on SR&ED staff by supervisors with scientific or technological qualifications; technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects claimed in the year (such as assigning technological personnel, setting job priorities, developing technological strategies, or evaluating quality of experimental materials); and tasks performed by non-specialized employees (such as operating a machine required for an experiment or feeding raw materials into a machine) when directly supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications.

For non-specified employees (arm's-length employees), allowable SR&ED salary or wages for Section 37 purposes include basic salary and wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips, gratuities, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, commissions, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, inducements, non-competition payments, and taxable benefits under section 6 where there is a cash outlay or a reasonable estimate of actual employer cost (excluding any GST/HST or PST component for which an Input Tax Credit can be claimed, as subsection 248(16) deems input tax credits to be government assistance).

Conversely, the following items are excluded from SR&ED salary or wages for all employees: (i) the employer's share of related benefits (such as employer contributions to CPP, EI, or group health insurance plans, which may only be claimed as Line 360 overhead under the Traditional Method or covered by the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method); (ii) stock option benefits under section 7 of the Act; (iii) extended vacation or extended sick leave; (iv) retiring allowances (which may only be claimed as Line 360 overhead under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental based on career SR&ED service ratio); and (v) unpaid remuneration under subsection 78(4)—any employee remuneration accrued in the taxation year that is not paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that year. Furthermore, even when prior-year unpaid salary is paid in a subsequent year and claimed on Line 310 of Form T661, it is permanently excluded from the Proxy Method Salary Base under Regulation 2900(9).
2. Specified Employee Statutory Ceilings (Subsection 37(9.1) and Regulation 2900(7)–(8))

A "specified employee" is defined in subsection 248(1) as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a specified shareholder owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation. 4.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

Under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V), Regulation 2900(2)(a), and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated March 27, 2026), claimants under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods may claim 100% of the cost of materials consumed (Line 320) or materials transformed (Line 325) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

For CRA audit purposes, "materials for SR&ED" refers strictly to physical and tangible raw materials, substances, or component items (existing in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of a tangible "thing" on which SR&ED is being performed or that results from the SR&ED. Eligible examples include metals and galvanization service costs for parts subjected to experimental testing, chemicals applied to wood samples, seeds, agar, fungal cultures, and incremental fertilizers or pesticides used on experimental test plots, and electronic components incorporated into an experimental prototype. Conversely, intangible items (software licences, datasets), general laboratory glassware and supplies (petri dishes, beakers, pipettes, flasks), cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, used lubricants, and general utilities (water, electricity, natural gas, unless consumed directly as a reactant in an endothermic or metallurgical process) do not compose the body of the experimental object and cannot be claimed as SR&ED materials. Under the Traditional Method, broken lab supplies and variable utilities may be claimed as Line 360 overhead; under the Proxy Method, they are covered by the 55% PPA.

Materials consumed (Line 320) are materials destroyed, absorbed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED (having less than 10% scrap value) and do not attract ITC recapture. Materials transformed (Line 325) are materials incorporated into another tangible property (such as a trial prototype, experimental production run, custom product, or commercial asset) that retains commercial value after the SR&ED concludes. If that resulting property is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 taxation years, the ITC earned on the materials transformed is subject to ITC Recapture under subsection 127(27). Materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED—never when merely purchased, received from a supplier, or held in inventory—and must be paid within the taxation year or within 180 days after year-end to earn an ITC. If materials are purchased from a non-arm's length supplier, the Section 127 qualified expenditure is capped by subsection 127(11.6) at the actual cost incurred by the non-arm's length supplier (stripping out any intercompany profit margin on Line 541).
4.4 Subcontractors (SR&ED Performed on Behalf) and Third-Party Payments

Canadian businesses frequently engage external contractors, engineering firms, universities, or research hospitals to perform portions of their R&D. The Income Tax Act draws statutory distinctions based on whether the performer is arm's length or non-arm's length (section 251), whether the work is a contract for SR&ED performed on behalf of the claimant (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)) versus a third-party payment (subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) and (ii)), and whether the work is performed inside or outside Canada.
1. Arm's-Length vs. Non-Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts (Contract Expenditures Policy)

Where a claimant pays an arm's-length taxable supplier (a person or partnership resident in Canada or carrying on business through a Canadian permanent establishment) to perform SR&ED (or paragraph (d) support work directly in support of the claimant's Canadian SR&ED) on the claimant's behalf in Canada (Line 340), 100% of the contract expenditure enters the payer's Section 37 deductible pool, and 80% enters the payer's Section 127 qualified expenditures to earn ITCs (with 20% subtracted on Line 529 of Form T661). For the arm's-length contractor performing the work, the amount received from the payer is a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9), which reduces the contractor's own qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar on a project-by-project basis under subsections 127(18) and 127(19). However, if the contractor's actual eligible SR&ED costs on the project exceed the contract payment received, the contractor may claim an SR&ED ITC on its uncompensated cost overrun. Additionally, if the arm's-length contractor was hired to perform only paragraph (d) support work, the payer can claim the contract (at 80% for ITCs), whereas the contractor cannot claim SR&ED on support work alone.

Where a claimant subcontracts SR&ED to a non-arm's length (NAL) party (Line 345), the payer may include 100% of the contract payment in its Section 37 deductible pool, but the contract payment is 0% eligible for the payer's Section 127 qualified expenditures. Instead, the NAL payment is not treated as a "contract payment" to the NAL performer, allowing the NAL performer to claim its own underlying SR&ED salaries, PPA, and materials to earn the ITC. Alternatively, the NAL performer and NAL payer may execute a joint agreement on Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(13) to transfer all or part of the performer's qualified expenditures (up to the contract amount) to the payer. An anti-avoidance rule in paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) prevents companies from interposing an arm's-length intermediary between two NAL corporations to bypass this restriction.

Between 2014 and December 15, 2024, when capital expenditures were ineligible for SR&ED, subsections 37(14) and 37(15) required a payer to reduce its SR&ED contract expenditure by any capital expenditures incurred by the contractor to fulfil the contract, and required the contractor to notify the payer in writing within 90 days of calendar year-end. Consequential to restoring SR&ED capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b), Bill C-15 repealed subsections 37(14) and 37(15) effective for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024. Finally, payments to foreign contractors performing R&D outside Canada cannot be claimed on Form T661 and earn 0% ITC (though current foreign R&D expenses remain deductible in computing ordinary business income under subsection 37(2)).
2. Third-Party Payments (Third-Party Payments Policy and Form T1263)

Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) and 37(1)(a)(ii), a claimant may claim Third-Party Payments (Line 370 of Form T661, supported by Form T1263, Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) made to six statutory categories of entities (Entities A through F: Canadian resident corporations [Entity A], approved associations [Entity B], approved universities, colleges, or research institutes [Entity C], paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit SR&ED corporations [Entity D and Entity F], and approved granting councils [Entity E]). Like arm's-length contracts, 100% of a qualifying third-party payment enters the Section 37 pool and 80% enters Section 127 qualified expenditures.

1. The "Directly Related and Incremental" Test for Traditional Overhead (Regulation 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3))

Claimants electing the Traditional Method may claim SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and Regulations 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3) only if each expense satisfies two cumulative statutory tests. First, under the "Directly Related" test, there must be a direct linkage—with no intervening step or intermediary—between the expenditure and (i) the SR&ED work itself, (ii) the SR&ED staff, or (iii) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform the SR&ED. For example, the employer's share of CPP/EI/benefits for hands-on SR&ED engineers is directly linked to SR&ED staff and is eligible; conversely, the employer's share of CPP/EI/benefits (or training and travel costs) for clerical or HR staff who support the SR&ED engineers has an intervening step and is ineligible. Second, under the "Incremental" test, the expenditure must be one that would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred. Variable costs that fluctuate directly with equipment usage (such as $100,000 of electricity on a plant line used 10% of the time for SR&ED, yielding $10,000 of incremental overhead) or clerical staff time (e.g., 5 clerks each spending 20% of their time on SR&ED purchasing or payroll, where 1 FTE clerk's salary is incremental) satisfy the test. By contrast, fixed costs—such as a fixed-cost annual equipment maintenance contract, fixed monthly telephone or internet base charges, corporate management, finance, or legal salaries, or headhunter and recruitment advertising fees—would have been incurred regardless of SR&ED and fail the incremental test (though employee relocation/moving expenses to transfer an SR&ED worker to another facility within Canada can qualify). Similarly, waste disposal costs qualify only during the active prosecution of SR&ED, not after the SR&ED activity has finished.
2. Cloud Computing (AWS, Azure) and Software Development Costs

In software, artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML) claims, cloud computing expenses (such as AWS or Azure infrastructure) require careful classification under CRA rules. First, because cloud computing instances, SaaS licences, and datasets are intangible and do not exist in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state composing a physical object, they cannot be claimed on Line 320/325 as SR&ED materials. Second, production hosting costs for commercial SaaS customers are routine operating expenses (paragraph 248(1)(i)) and must be excluded, while staging and QA environments must be allocated between development and commercial operations. Third, when a software company elects the Proxy Method, general cloud utilities, internet, and overhead expenses are covered by the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and are deducted as ordinary business expenses under section 9(1). Under the Traditional Method, incremental, variable cloud computing usage directly tied to running experimental development environments or training experimental ML models (above fixed baseline service charges) can be claimed as directly related and incremental Line 360 overhead. Additionally, where dedicated physical development servers or hardware are acquired or leased after December 15, 2024 and used 90% or more (ASA) or more than 50% (primarily) for SR&ED in Canada, they qualify under the restored capital expenditure, SUE, or equipment lease provisions.
3. Prescribed Expenditures Excluded by Regulation 2902

Even if an expenditure is directly related and incremental to SR&ED, section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations designates specific outlays as prescribed expenditures that are excluded from Section 127 qualified expenditures. These prescribed exclusions encompass fees for preparing SR&ED claims (professional or internal fees paid to prepare SR&ED tax incentive claims, which are deductible only as ordinary business expenses), costs to attend conventions or conferences, interest and borrowing expenses, expenditures to acquire rights in or arising out of SR&ED (subsection 37(4) and Regulation 2902(c)), and used depreciable capital property (Regulation 2902(b), subtracted on Line 532).
4.6 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), Lease Costs, Asset Development, and Recapture (Post-December 15, 2024)

Between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures and equipment lease costs were excluded from the federal SR&ED program. Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment, and equipment lease costs effective for property acquired (and available for use) or lease amounts first becoming payable after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024), as codified in the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), and SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026).
1. SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b) — The 90% ASA Rule)

An expenditure on depreciable property acquired and available for use (under subsections 37(1.2) and 127(11.2)) after December 15, 2024 qualifies as an SR&ED Capital Expenditure (reported on Line 390 and Part 6B, Boxes 780, 782, and 786 of Form T661) if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended either (i) to use the property during all or substantially all (ASA — defined as 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or (ii) to consume all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of the property's value in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

Capital cost includes the purchase price, installation costs, customs and excise duties, transportation, and other direct acquisition costs (excluding borrowing/interest costs). When claimed on Line 390 of Form T661, the property must not be included on Schedule 8 for regular CCA. Both new and used ASA depreciable property (other than general-purpose office equipment or furniture [GPOEF] under the Proxy Method) qualify for 100% immediate deduction in the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(b). However, for Section 127 ITC purposes, used property is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902(b) and must be subtracted on Line 532 of Form T661, earning 0% ITC. The only exception is where used equipment is refurbished by a vendor prior to acquisition to such a significant extent (replacing or rebuilding major parts to bring it to the current state of the art) that it is considered "new when acquired," or where the claimant incurs refurbishment costs after December 15, 2024 on its own equipment (in which case the refurbishment costs themselves qualify). Land is non-depreciable and never qualifies, while buildings and leasehold interests in buildings are excluded by paragraph 37(8)(e) unless the building is a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 2903.
2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Subsection 127(9) — The 25% + 25% Rule)

When new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 does not meet the 90% ASA threshold, it cannot enter the Section 37 pool and must be depreciated under regular CCA rules on T2 Schedule 8. However, if the equipment is used primarily (defined as more than 50% and less than 90% of its actual operating time) for SR&ED in Canada, it qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (reported on Line 504 and Part 6C, Boxes 788–796 of Form T661) to earn Section 127 ITCs in two tranches:

items: First-Term SUE (25% of Capital Cost): If the property is new, not GPOEF, and not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP under Regulation 2900(11), which excludes equipment intended at acquisition to be used during commercial plant assembly, construction, or commissioning and thereafter primarily for non-SR&ED commercial manufacturing), and its actual SR&ED operating time is more than 50% during the first period (starting on the date the equipment becomes available for use and ending at the end of the first taxation year that ends at least 12 months after that date), 25% (1/4) of the capital cost is deemed to be a qualified expenditure earning an ITC in that taxation year. (If the equipment is acquired mid-year so that less than 12 months elapse before the first year-end, the first-term SUE claim occurs at the second taxation year-end).

Second-Term SUE (Additional 25% of Capital Cost): If the equipment qualified as first-term SUE and its cumulative actual SR&ED operating time is more than 50% during the second period (starting on the date the equipment became available for use and ending at the end of the first taxation year that ends at least 24 months after that date), an additional 25% (1/4) of the capital cost (bringing the total to 50% of capital cost) qualifies for an ITC in that subsequent taxation year. Any ITC claimed or refunded on SUE reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of its Schedule 8 CCA class in the subsequent taxation year.

body.text: 3. Restored Equipment Lease Expenditures (Incurred After December 15, 2024)

Under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)–(II) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) & (VI), lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada qualify as current SR&ED expenditures (and earn 100% Section 127 ITC inclusion) based on operating time. If leased equipment is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost is claimable on Line 350 under both the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method (excluding GPOEF under the Proxy Method). If leased equipment is used more than 50% but less than 90% (primarily) of its operating time for SR&ED, a claimant using the Proxy Method claims 50% of the lease cost (excluding GPOEF) on Line 355, whereas a claimant using the Traditional Method claims the proportional SR&ED usage percentage on Line 360 as overhead (provided it is directly related and incremental). If leased equipment is used 50% or less of its operating time for SR&ED, 0% is claimable under the Proxy Method, while the proportional SR&ED percentage may be claimed on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental. Building rent is excluded under both methods (subparagraph 37(8)(d)(ii)) except for prescribed special-purpose buildings, and land leases are excluded under the Proxy Method but allowable under the Traditional Method if ASA or directly attributable to SR&ED.
4. Pilot Plants, Commercial Plants, Prototypes, Custom Products, and the 20-Year ITC Recapture Window

Under the CRA's SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy and Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (subsections 127(27) to 127(36)), a pilot plant is a non-commercial facility isolated from regular business operations and developed for the primary purpose of carrying out SR&ED during its useful life; current expenditures (labour, materials consumed or transformed, contracts, and overhead) to develop and operate it qualify. Conversely, a facility intended for temporary or permanent conversion to commercial operations is a commercial plant, for which only segregated, incremental current costs directly addressing technological uncertainties qualify. Where it is difficult to apportion expenses between SR&ED work and commercial work on a custom product or commercial asset, the CRA permits the Alternative Approach:

Allowable SR&ED expenditures = Total actual costs incurred to develop the asset − Estimated cost to develop the asset had the technology already existed + Estimated cost of materials transformed in SR&ED

If a claimant disposes of, or converts to commercial use, any property on which an SR&ED ITC was earned within the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years to 20 years by subsection 127(36))—specifically materials transformed into a custom product or prototype, ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment (when SR&ED usage becomes purely incidental), or non-IP physical property acquired under an SR&ED contract—the claimant must add a Recaptured ITC under subsection 127(27) directly to its Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion. The recapture amount is the lesser of (i) the original SR&ED ITC earned on the cost of the property, and (ii) the applicable ITC rate (35% or 15%, or 20% for pre-2014 claims) multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (if sold at arm's length) or the Fair Market Value (FMV) of the property at the time of commercial conversion or non-arm's length disposition. Recapture never applies to SR&ED salaries, wages, or overhead imputed to a custom product; never applies to the disposition or commercialization of Intellectual Property (IP); and never applies under the de minimis rule if scrap proceeds or FMV upon conversion are less than 10% of the total cost of the property. Any ITC recaptured in Year T is added back to the claimant's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in Year T+1 under paragraph 37(1)(c.2) (Line 453 of Form T661).

body.text: 5.2 Deep-Dive of Key Provincial Regimes
1. Ontario's Three-Credit Architecture (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)

(Note: Certain third-party marketing blogs erroneously state that Ontario offers a 20% OITC and 10% ORDTC or that the ORDTC is capped at $500,000. Official CRA and Ontario authorities confirm that for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016, the OITC rate is 8%, the ORDTC rate is 3.5%, the OBRITC rate is 20%, and the ORDTC has no expenditure cap.)

Ontario administers three distinct corporate R&D tax credits through the CRA on the T2 corporate return. The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — 8% Refundable, Schedule 566) is available to corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to a $3,000,000 annual expenditure limit (shared among associated corporations), generating up to $240,000 in cash refunds. While the federal expenditure limit doubled to $6,000,000 under Bill C-15, Ontario's OITC expenditure limit remains $3,000,000, and phases out when the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income lies between $500,000 and $800,000 or prior-year Ontario specified capital lies between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

The Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — 3.5% Non-Refundable, Schedule 508) is available to all corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment regardless of size or foreign ownership and has no expenditure limit. To prevent double-counting on the first $3,000,000 of spending, the 8% OITC entitlement (along with other government assistance) is subtracted from gross eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures before multiplying by 3.5%. Unused ORDTC carries back 3 years and forward 20 years. A corporation in a tax-loss position may waive all or part of its ORDTC (or OITC) by delivering a written waiver with its return within 6 months of year-end (or on an amended return) so that an unutilized non-refundable credit does not unnecessarily reduce its federal SR&ED expenditure pool as government assistance. Finally, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — 20% Refundable, Schedules 568 & 569) provides a 20% refundable credit on up to $20,000,000 of qualified expenditures (maximum credit of $4,000,000 per year) incurred under an eligible contract with an Ontario university, college of applied arts and technology, hospital research institute, or Ontario Centre of Excellence.
2. Québec's Transformation: The Consolidated CRIC Regime (Effective After March 25, 2025)

In its March 25, 2025 Budget (Information Bulletin 2025-6, implemented via Québec Bill 6, substantively enacted November 11, 2025 and enacted December 12, 2025), the Government of Québec executed a sweeping overhaul of its provincial R&D tax incentives. For taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, Revenu Québec confirmed the elimination of seven legacy innovation tax measures: (1) the tax credit for salaries and wages of researchers (Form RD-1029.7-V), (2) the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or a research consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), (3) the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V), (4) the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V), (5) the tax credit for technological adaptation services, (6) the industrial design component of the design tax credits (while fashion design remains eligible), and (7) the tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts. They are replaced by the single, consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), claimed by corporations on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T.

The CRIC provides a 100% refundable tax credit to all eligible corporations (whether CCPCs, public corporations, or foreign-owned subsidiaries operating a business with an establishment in Québec) at a two-tier rate structure independent of corporate asset size: 30% refundable on the first $1,000,000 of qualified R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold, and 20% refundable on all qualified expenditures above that $1,000,000 bracket. For a given taxation year, a corporation's qualified expenditures must exceed an annual Exclusion Threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec Basic Personal Amount (BPA) under the applicable personal income tax system for each eligible employee (which is $18,952 per FTE employee for 2026, compared to $18,571 / $18,751 in 2025), adjusted to reflect the percentage of time each employee spent on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities. For example, if a Québec corporation has $1,500,000 in eligible salaries across 25 employees and a prorated exclusion threshold of $355,350, its net qualified expenditures of $1,144,650 earn a refundable CRIC of ($1,000,000 × 30%) + ($144,650 × 20%) = $300,000 + $28,930 = $328,930.

In addition to core R&D (which remains harmonized with the federal subsection 248(1) definition and continues to undergo scientific review by the CRA), the CRIC covers pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec in conjunction with and as a continuation of Québec R&D. Eligible pre-commercialization activities include tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements and obtain an initial approval or certification for commercializing an innovation; product design (including development of form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials); and quality control activities only where related to implementing a quality control system required to obtain initial approval or certification. CRIC qualified expenditures comprise 100% of direct employee salaries and wages, 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for a contract carried out in Québec, 50% of payments made to an eligible Québec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity, and 100% of property acquisition costs for capital equipment used in R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec (excluding land, buildings, rights to use land or buildings, property claimed under the C3i tax credit, or property used in a large investment project tax holiday). Unlike the federal Proxy Method, the CRIC does not provide a proxy overhead multiplier.
3. British Columbia, Alberta, and Saskatchewan Updates

In British Columbia, Budget 2026 and Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026, which received Royal Assent on April 16, 2026) removed the statutory sunset date to make the 10% BC SR&ED Tax Credit (Form T666) permanent. Effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, BC harmonized with federal Bill C-15: it doubled the BC refundable expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (increasing the maximum annual refundable BC credit from $300,000 to $600,000), extended the 10% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) alongside CCPCs, adopted the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 prior-year taxable capital phase-out, and restored the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures.

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG — AT1 Schedule 29) provides a refundable grant delivered through the Alberta corporate tax system on up to $4,000,000 of annual Alberta R&D expenditures incurred after December 31, 2020 that match federal SR&ED criteria. It pays 8% on Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base spending level (calculated as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding 2 taxation years) and 20% on incremental Alberta R&D spending exceeding that 2-year average base, yielding a maximum annual benefit of $800,000. The IEG phases out incrementally for firms with between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 in taxable capital, and disbursements are processed once qualifying expenses are verified by the CRA and confirmed in Alberta by the Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA).

In Saskatchewan, under section 63.4 of The Income Tax Act, 2000 (Schedule 403), effective December 16, 2024, Saskatchewan doubled the annual qualifying expenditure limit on which CCPCs earn a 10% refundable R&D tax credit from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 (yielding up to $200,000 in cash refunds, plus a 10% non-refundable credit on qualifying expenditures exceeding $2,000,000 and for non-CCPCs, up to a combined annual credit cap of $1,000,000).
5.3 Provincial Patent Box and IP Commercialization Regimes (Québec IDCI & Saskatchewan SCII)
While Canada has not enacted a federal patent box regime, two provinces operate statutory intellectual property (IP) commercialization tax incentives that complement front-end SR&ED credits.

In Québec, under the Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations in Québec (IDCI — Form CO-737.18.CI), applicable to taxation years beginning after December 31, 2020, corporations commercializing a qualified intellectual property asset in Québec may claim a taxable income deduction on Form CO-737.18.CI that reduces the effective Québec corporate income tax rate on qualified IP income from the general 11.5% rate down to 2.0%.

In Saskatchewan, under The Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive (Patent Box) Act (S.S. 2017, c. S-10.2) and section 64.6 of The Income Tax Act, 2000, the Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive (SCII) reduces the provincial corporate income tax rate to 6.0% (down from the 12.0% general corporate rate) on income derived from commercializing qualifying intellectual property—including patents, plant breeders' rights, trade secrets, and copyrights that pass a scientific eligibility test and are new to the Canadian market. The 6.0% reduced rate applies for 10 consecutive taxation years, or 15 consecutive taxation years if at least 50% of the related R&D was conducted in Saskatchewan, and the corporation may choose when to start its benefit period to align with peak IP revenue. Following Bill 158 in May 2024 (which extended the subsection 5(5) period from 7 years to 8 years), Saskatchewan enacted Bill 17 (The Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive (Patent Box) Amendment Act, 2025, Royal Assent May 13, 2025), which removed the economic eligibility test and extended the SCII application intake sunset by two years to June 30, 2027.
Section 6: Direct Innovation Grants, Clean Economy ITCs, and Government Assistance Stacking Mechanics
6.1 NRC Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) & Strategic Response Fund (SRF / SIF)

Canadian R&D performers frequently combine retrospective SR&ED tax credits with prospective direct government grants. The two flagship federal direct R&D funding instruments are the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) / Strategic Response Fund (SRF).

Operating since 1962 with more than 250–260 Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs) across Canada, NRC IRAP provides non-repayable financial contributions (grants) to incorporated, for-profit businesses operating in Canada that have 500 or fewer full-time equivalent (FTE) employees globally across the corporate group. According to the NRC 2024–25 Departmental Results Report, NRC IRAP provided $393.1 million to 3,136 SMEs in FY2024–25, and Budget 2026 proposed $298 million over three years from 2027–28 ($65 million, $107 million, and $126 million) to renew NRC IRAP's Clean Technology initiative. While NRC IRAP's official program pages do not publish a single fixed funding percentage, its service standards cover project contributions up to $10,000,000, and industry guides report typical reimbursement rates of up to 80% of eligible internal technical employee salary costs and up to 50% of eligible arm's-length subcontractor costs (subject to a 75% total combined government assistance ceiling). Unlike SR&ED, NRC IRAP is strictly non-retroactive: any work started or costs incurred before the formal IRAP Contribution Agreement is signed are disqualified.

For large-scale capital and innovation projects, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) administers the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF)—which has transitioned into the Strategic Response Fund (SRF) to blend trade-exposed tariff resilience with innovation in advanced manufacturing, clean tech, critical minerals, defence/dual-use, semiconductors, biomanufacturing, and aerospace. The SRF targets projects with at least $20,000,000+ in total eligible costs and a minimum $10,000,000+ federal contribution, providing up to an approximate 50% cost-share through a mix of repayable and non-repayable contributions. Under the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, any government contribution where repayment is conditional on future revenues, profits, or milestones (such as a forgivable or conditionally repayable SIF/SRF loan) is legally treated as government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9) in the year received or receivable, reducing both the Section 37 pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures. Only when the corporation actually repays the contribution in future taxation years are those repayments added back to the Section 37 pool (Line 445) and Line 560 to generate non-refundable ITCs.

6.3 Exact Mathematical Mechanics of Government Assistance Stacking

Under paragraph 37(1)(d), subsection 127(9), and subsection 127(18), provincial R&D tax credits and direct federal or provincial grants (such as NRC IRAP) are government assistance that must be subtracted from qualified SR&ED expenditures on a project-by-project basis. On April 1, 2026, pursuant to the legislative modernization enacted in Bill C-15, the CRA launched its formal, optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (detailed in CRA Information Sheet Cat. Rv4-224/2026E-PD and Form T1322, Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Pre-Claim Approval). This program allows businesses to obtain an official technical eligibility determination from the CRA before starting an R&D project or incurring costs.

To qualify to apply, a business must operate in Canada, have less than $25,000,000 in annual gross business income, be a CCPC, other Canadian corporation, or partnership, and be in good standing with the CRA. Each application on Form T1322 can cover up to 3 planned SR&ED projects, which must represent new work not already claimed and not involve issues under formal objection or litigation. Once granted, pre-claim approval can cover a project for up to 3 taxation years, subject to program conditions. The application workflow proceeds through five sequential steps:

items: Request a Case Number: The business completes a brief online web form providing a contact name, legal business name, and Business Number; the CRA contacts existing claimants in good standing within 2 business days through My Business Account (and other applicants within 5 business days by telephone).

Apply in My Business Account (Form T1322): The business completes Form T1322 (Parts 1 to 3, Lines 010 to 082, including Section C identifying who prepared the responses) for up to 3 projects and uploads supporting project documentation.
Meet an SR&ED Specialist: New claimants are contacted, and existing claimants may be contacted, to schedule a virtual meeting with an SR&ED specialist.

Receive a Formal Determination Within 8 Weeks: The CRA issues its written determination within 8 weeks of receiving a complete application deciding whether the planned projects meet the subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED.

File Annual Form T661 After Performing the Work: Pre-claim approval determines the eligibility of proposed work, not the final quantum of allowable expenditures. 7.4 CRA Service Standards, Audit Review Process, FTCAS, and Dispute Resolution

Under the CRA's After You Claim guidance (updated October 14, 2026) and The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), the CRA maintains three processing service standards (aimed to be met 90% of the time) for refundable SR&ED claims: 60 calendar days for refundable claims accepted as filed without review; 90 calendar days for refundable claims selected for an expenditure-only review where all claimed projects were granted Pre-Claim Approval; and 180 calendar days for refundable claims selected for review that include any project not granted pre-claim approval (or that materially differed from what was pre-approved). Non-refundable SR&ED claims have no formal processing service standard.

If a business is filing its first SR&ED claim, or has not submitted a claim in the last 3 years, it may be selected for the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS). FTCAS is a mandatory virtual service for selected claimants, but it is not an audit or review: no determinations on work eligibility or allowable expenditures are made during FTCAS, any expected refund is processed after the online meeting takes place, and the claimant receives a written follow-up report with customized recommendations to support future claims.

When a claim is selected for a formal technical and financial review, it cannot be withdrawn: the certification signed in Part 10 of Form T661 is an irrevocable part of the tax return. Reviews are conducted virtually (or on-site on an exceptional, case-by-case basis) by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (who evaluates whether the work meets the subsection 248(1) definition, interviews hands-on personnel, examines contemporaneous records, and authors the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, reporting to a Research and Technology Manager, RTM) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (who audits general ledgers, payroll, timesheets, contracts, and 180-day payment proof, reporting to a Financial Review Manager, FRM). When negative adjustments are proposed, the CRA issues a Proposal Package (containing the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, proposal letter, financial adjustments, and any proposed penalties), and the claimant has 30 calendar days from the date of the proposal letter to submit written representations and additional supporting documentation.
The Five-Stage Dispute Resolution, Objection, and Judicial Appeal Escalation Pathway

items: Stage 1 — Direct Discussion with Reviewers: Raise technical or financial concerns directly with the assigned Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and/or Financial Reviewer (FR) as early as possible.
Stage 2 — Escalation to Review Management: If unresolved, escalate the issue to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM).

Stage 3 — Formal Administrative Review (Form RC532): After receiving the Proposal Package and before the 30-day response period expires and the file is closed, the claimant may submit Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Review) to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (Business Tax Incentives Directorate, Enterprise Building, 13th Floor, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa, ON K1A 0L5). Forwarded within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director, the Administrative Review checks whether the claimant received due process and whether the review complied with current SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures, resulting in either Decision Maintained or Decision Reconsidered.

Stage 4 — Formal Notice of Objection to CRA Appeals Branch (90 Days): Once a Notice of Assessment, Reassessment, or Determination is issued, the claimant has 90 calendar days from the date of the Notice to file a formal Notice of Objection (Form RC592 or Form T400A, or online via My Business Account / Represent a Client) with the Chief of Appeals at the Appeals Intake Centre (for individuals other than trusts, the deadline is the later of 90 days from the Notice or 1 year after the T1 filing deadline). If the corporation is a "large corporation" (total taxable capital employed in Canada with related corporations exceeding $10,000,000), the Notice of Objection must specifically describe each issue, specify the exact dollar relief sought for each issue, and the corporation must pay 50% of the disputed amount while the objection is pending.

Stage 5 — Judicial Appeals to the Courts: If the claimant disagrees with the CRA Appeals Branch's Notice of Confirmation or Reassessment (or if 90 days have elapsed since filing the Notice of Objection without a CRA decision), the claimant may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) within 90 calendar days of the CRA's decision. From a final judgment of the Tax Court of Canada, an appeal lies to the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) within 30 days (excluding July and August), and thereafter by application for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada (SCC) within 60 days (excluding July).

1. Part 9 Claim Preparer Information Penalty (Subsections 162(5.1) to (5.3) — $1,000 Joint Liability)

In Part 9 of Form T661 (Lines 935 to 975), every claimant must disclose complete information for each "claim preparer" that accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the SR&ED claim, including the preparer's name, Business Number, billing arrangement code (e.g., contingency fee), billing rate, and total fee. Even if no claim preparer assisted with the claim, the claimant must still complete Lines 935, 970, and 975 in Part 9. Under subsection 162(5.1) of the Income Tax Act, if required claim preparer information in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable (subject to the due diligence defence under subsection 162(5.2)).
2. Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims (Subsection 163(2) & Paragraph 163(2)(d))

Under subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), any person who, knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes, participates in, assents to, or accepts a false statement or omission in an initial or amended return or Form T661 is liable to a civil penalty. Under subsection 163(3), the burden of proof rests on the CRA to establish on a balance of probabilities that the false statement or omission resulted from more than a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the Act.

The CRA considers applying the gross negligence penalty when a claimant participates in overstating SR&ED amounts, includes projects known not to involve SR&ED, describes SR&ED activities that did not occur, or continues to claim non-qualifying projects, miscalculations, or unsubstantiated expenditures after being advised in writing by the CRA that they do not qualify (where no objection or appeal is active). The amount of the penalty is the greater of $100 or 50% of the sum of: (1) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (under paragraph 163(2)(a), where overstated expenditures and overstated ITCs are deemed deducted first), plus (2) the refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed by the taxpayer (under paragraph 163(2)(d)).

As documented in Sections 4.3, 5.2, and 5.3 of the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy, there is a critical statutory difference between paragraph 163(2)(a) (when an overstated ITC is deducted against Part I tax payable) and paragraph 163(2)(d) (when an overstated refundable ITC is claimed as a cash refund): when the gross negligence penalty applies to the refund of a refundable ITC under paragraph 163(2)(d), the CRA calculates the 50% penalty on the entire overstated refund claimed, even if part of that overstatement resulted from an innocent oversight.
